metadata.name: journalctl
metadata.description: Query and display messages from the systemd journal

installation.note: journalctl is part of systemd, built-in on modern Linux distributions (Ubuntu 15.04+, Debian 8+)

overview.summary: journalctl queries and displays messages from the systemd journal, which is the centralized logging system on modern Linux systems. It provides powerful filtering and searching capabilities for system logs, service logs, and kernel messages.
when_to_use: View logs from a specific time period

syntax.description: Query the systemd journal. Can filter by unit, priority, time, and more.

options.description: Show logs for a specific systemd unit (service)
options.use_case: View logs for a specific service only
Watch logs in real-time as new entries appear

options.description: Show the last N log entries
options.use_case: See only the most recent log entries

options.description: Filter by priority level (emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug)
options.use_case: Show only error-level messages and above
View logs from a specific time period

options.description: Show logs from current or specified boot
options.use_case: See only logs from the current boot session

common_misconceptions.title: journalctl replaces all log files
common_misconceptions.misconception: Traditional log files in /var/log are gone
common_misconceptions.reality: Many services still write to /var/log, but systemd services use the journal. journalctl provides unified access to systemd logs.
common_misconceptions.tip: Use journalctl for systemd services, check /var/log for traditional applications

common_misconceptions.title: All logs are permanent
common_misconceptions.misconception: All journal entries are kept forever
common_misconceptions.reality: Journal has size limits and rotates. Old entries are automatically deleted based on configuration.
common_misconceptions.tip: Check journal size with 'journalctl --disk-usage' and configure retention in /etc/systemd/journald.conf

common_pitfalls.description: Running journalctl without filters shows all logs, which can be overwhelming
common_pitfalls.solution: Always use filters: -u for service, -n for last N lines, --since for time range, -p for priority

common_pitfalls.description: Old journal entries may have been rotated out
common_pitfalls.solution: Check journal retention settings. Use --since with specific dates to see what's available

best_practices: Always use filters to narrow down results (-u, -n, --since, -p)
Use -f to follow logs when debugging active issues
Combine filters: journalctl -u nginx -p err --since today
performance_tips: Use specific filters to reduce output and improve performance
Limit output with -n when you only need recent entries
Use --since to avoid processing old log entries
For production, configure journal retention in /etc/systemd/journald.conf

related_commands.description: Use systemctl to control services, journalctl to view their logs
journalctl -k provides similar functionality to dmesg but with better filtering
journalctl -f is the systemd equivalent of tail -f for traditional log files

additional_notes.note1: Journal logs are stored in binary format for efficiency. journalctl converts them to readable text.
additional_notes.note2: Use 'journalctl --list-boots' to see available boot sessions
additional_notes.note3: Journal can be configured to forward to syslog or store logs persistently in /var/log/journal
